content: Recurrent apnea is a frequent condition in preterm infants, especially those born at very early gestational ages. This condition can result in hypoxemia (low blood oxygen levels) and bradycardia (slowed heart rate), which, in severe cases, may necessitate resuscitation measures such as positive pressure ventilation. Doxapram has been utilized as a respiratory stimulant to mitigate apnea and its associated complications. The objective of this study was to assess the efficacy of doxapram in reducing apnea episodes and the need for intermittent positive airway pressure (IPPV) in preterm infants experiencing recurrent apnea. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE (from 1966 to April 2009), EMBASE (from 1980 to April 2009), and CINAHL (from 1982 to April 2009). The search terms included doxapram, apnea or apnoea, and the MeSH term infant, premature. Additionally, prior reviews, cross-references, conference abstracts, and symposia proceedings were examined. Abstracts from the Society for Pediatric Research (1996–2008) were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria for this analysis were randomized or quasi-randomized trials in which doxapram was administered to treat apnea in preterm infants. Each study was independently assessed by the review authors for quality and eligibility, and data were extracted accordingly. Only one trial met the inclusion criteria. This trial involved 21 preterm infants, with 11 randomized to receive intravenous doxapram and 10 assigned to a placebo group. After 48 hours of treatment, fewer treatment failures were observed in the doxapram group (4 out of 11 infants) compared to the placebo group (8 out of 10 infants). However, the wide confidence intervals rendered this result statistically non-significant (summary relative risk: 0.45, 95% CI: 0.20 to 1.05). Only one infant in the placebo group required IPPV. Among the 11 infants treated with doxapram, seven initially responded within the first 48 hours. However, five of these responders experienced treatment failure between 48 hours and seven days after starting therapy, resulting in a late failure rate of 9 out of 11. This late failure rate was comparable to the short-term failure rate observed in the placebo group (8 out of 10). It was not possible to evaluate the late responses of all infants in the placebo group, as they were subsequently crossed over to a treatment arm. The authors concluded that while intravenous doxapram may reduce apnea episodes within the first 48 hours of treatment, the available data are insufficient to confirm the reliability of this finding or to evaluate potential adverse effects. Furthermore, no long-term outcomes were assessed in the study. Additional research is necessary to clarify the role of doxapram in clinical practice and to determine its safety and efficacy in the management of apnea in preterm infants.
